Your app didn’t crash because of a bug. It crashed because the Indian government decided to block your backend.

Starting February 24th, https://t.co/cpotyIe5BS became unreachable across major Indian ISPs. Supabase later confirmed this was due to a ministry order. No prior notice. No public explanation. No transition window.

Jio. Airtel. ACT Fibernet. All started DNS-poisoning Supabase domains, redirecting API calls to a sinkhole IP. Every app running on Supabase in India (auth, database, edge functions, real-time) went dark for millions of users. Reports suggest Firebase Hosting is facing similar disruptions.

Thousands of startups, student projects, hackathon builds, production SaaS apps. Blocked. No “here’s 90 days to migrate.” Nothing.

Supabase had to publicly tag Minister Ashwini Vaishnaw on X just to get someone to talk to them: “Supabase is used by millions of developers worldwide, and millions of users in India are currently unable to access our platform. Could we talk to someone in your team about this?”

Silence from MeitY. Silence from the Minister. Silence from every ISP.

Supabase is not a social media platform. It’s a PostgreSQL database wrapper with auth, storage, and APIs. Its users are engineers building software. There is no obvious legal or content-based reason to block it.

And this isn’t the first time. Medium blocked on Jio/Airtel in Oct 2025. Linktree blocked without explanation. BSNL blocked Dailymotion and Telegram links in Aug 2025. ACT Fibernet blocked TheMovieDB. Ubuntu mirrors and Cloudflare R2 hit before that.

Critical internet infrastructure keeps getting caught in opaque, unaccountable blocking orders. No public reasoning. No appeals process. No distinction between a piracy site and a developer tool.

The workaround? Switch DNS to 1.1.1.1 or 8.8.8.8. Use a VPN. Proxy backend traffic through custom domains so you’re not exposed to ISP blocks.

But think about what we’re saying. We’re telling Indian developers: “Your government might randomly block your backend, so architect around that.” That’s not a healthy ecosystem. That’s building on a minefield.

We talk about Digital India. Startup India. A $5 trillion economy. We want to compete globally in SaaS and AI.

But we’re blocking the tools our developers need to build. Without notice. Without reason. Without a plan.

India’s builders deserve better than this.

#Supabase #Firebase #MeitY #DigitalIndia #StartupIndia #NetNeutrality #Developers #IndianStartups

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

While the rule lists what a “reasoned intimation” should contain, the legal basis, statutory provision, nature of the unlawful act, and specific URL/identifier, the three-hour window pressures platforms to comply promptly which may often occur without any substantive assessment. These inherently opaque censorship practices are being accelerated through "Sahyog" portal. Developed by the Indian Cybercrime Coordination Centre (I4C), the Sahyog portal operates entirely without statutory footing, only being anchored in the IT Rules, 2021 that are created by executive notification. It functions as a censorship clearinghouse that deliberately bypasses the established, albeit weak, procedural safeguards of Section 69A. By routing automated takedown directives directly to intermediaries under Section 79(3)(b) of the IT Act, the portal structurally excludes citizens and impacted users from the grievance process.

We demand that the government introduce strictly judicially enforceable transparency requirements, publish all blocking orders, and restore the principles of natural justice to India's platform governance framework. Based on requests from our community we will also next week launch a rough public sheet in which social media users can input and add information on digital censorship.

*New Delhi, February 28, 2026*

The Internet Freedom Foundation (IFF) is concerned by a cluster of online blocking and takedown actions and ISP level service disruptions reported between 24–28 February 2026. Across these incidents, users and affected services face restrictions without clear, timely reasons and without access to the underlying orders needed to challenge state action by exercising their rights to obtain legal remedy.

Developers reported severe, uneven disruption in access to Supabase across multiple Indian networks. Reporting indicates the disruption followed a government direction, with accounts suggesting use of Section 69A of the Information Technology Act, 2000. Yet there has been no public statement of the grounds, scope, or duration, and no accessible order for those impacted. Supabase has publicly stated that its domains became inaccessible due to a “ministry order”, and users have been pushed to workarounds such as alternative DNS or VPNs. In parallel, users on X (formerly Twitter) continue to receive “withheld in India” notices restricting specific posts within the country. Such notices usually do not provide the government order or its reasoning. Hence, for those who are being censored the basics of natural justice of a notice, opportunity for a hearing and remedy are delayed or absent.

This is enabled by secrecy built into the blocking framework. Section 69A is implemented through the 2009 Blocking Rules, which contemplate a committee process and, where feasible, notice to intermediaries and identifiable originators. But they also impose “strict confidentiality” over requests and actions taken. When orders and reasons are secret by default, affected persons cannot test legality, necessity, proportionality, or factual errors except through protracted litigation. When in _Shreya Singhal v. Union of India_ (2015), the Supreme Court upheld Section 69A while relying on the existence of procedural safeguards and reasoned decisions, indicating that impacted users could approach court in writ remedies. However, due to the operational secrecy and providing copies of orders and notices those who are censored and prevented from obtaining judicial remedy.

Two members of Congress have been quietly merging two separate site-blocking bills into one.

Representative Zoe Lofgren (D) of California and Senator Thom Tillis (R) of North Carolina's bill would let copyright holders petition federal courts to order American internet service providers and DNS resolvers to block entire foreign domains.

Comcast. Verizon. Spectrum. T-Mobile. Cloudflare. Google. OpenDNS. All of them, ordered to refuse to resolve a domain on the strength of a court order obtained by the MPA's lawyers.

Once the law exists, any foreign domain a federal judge finds objectionable disappears from the address book of every American household that does not run its own resolver.

This is what fourteen years of post-SOPA institutional memory loss looks like.

In 2012, the Stop Online Piracy Act died on the floor of Congress because the public found out what was in it before it passed. Wikipedia went dark in protest. Reddit went dark. Google put a black censor bar across its homepage. The bill sponsors retreated. The lesson the entertainment industry took from that defeat was not that the public opposed internet censorship. The lesson was that public attention was the problem.

So this time the bill has been drafted in private. There has been no blackout. There has been no consumer-facing campaign. The strategy is to negotiate the details quietly with the parties most able to refuse, and the public never finds out the law exists until they cannot reach a website.

In early 2026, the Supreme Court ruled in Cox Communications v. Sony Music that an ISP cannot be held liable for a billion dollars because some of its customers downloaded music. Justice Sotomayor, in a concurrence, complained that the ruling now permits ISPs to sell internet access to "every single infringer who wants one" without lifting a finger to prevent infringement. The publishers and the studios read that as a green light to ask Congress for the lever the courts no longer hand them.

This is the lever they want. A federal court order. A list of foreign domains. ISPs and DNS resolvers compelled by law to block on receipt.

The list of countries that already have laws like this includes the United Kingdom, France, Italy, Spain, Australia, India, Brazil, and Russia. The MPA cites this as evidence that the United States is behind. In Spain, IP-level blocking ordered by the football league has knocked legitimate businesses offline because they happened to share a server with a blocked domain. In Italy, the Piracy Shield system has blocked Cloudflare entirely on multiple occasions. In the United Kingdom, blocking orders have been used to take down sites that were not piracy sites at all, on the basis that they linked to piracy sites.

The collateral damage is the system working as designed. The blunter the instrument, the easier the enforcement.

There is no version of this law that targets only the bad actors. Domains are not isolated. Hosting is shared. CDNs are shared. The address book is a single document. Once the law exists, the list of blocked domains will only grow, the criteria will only loosen, and the appeal process will only formalize what was already done.

Anything that depends on resolving a foreign domain becomes contingent on the goodwill of a federal court and the lobbying budget of whoever wants the domain alive. Every shadow library, every IPTV mirror, every privacy-respecting service whose lawyers cannot match Disney's. All of them will be one petition away from disappearing from the address book of every household whose internet runs through Comcast.

Most people do not run a VPN, do not configure a custom DNS, do not know what an IP address is. Most people get the internet their ISP serves them. The bill is written for those people. The bill assumes that if the road is closed at the resolver, the destination effectively does not exist.

This bill will outlive its sponsors, its pretext, and the industries that bought it. Laws granting infrastructure-level censorship power do not get repealed. They get expanded. Every kill switch finds a hand.

The Cockroach Janta Party, founded by Aam Aadmi Party (AAP) member Abhijeet Dipke, has compromised the sensitive personal information of people who were misled into believing that he was fighting for the cause of ‘students’ in the aftermath of the NEET paper leak.

For the unversed, Dipke had called upon his followers to register on his party’s website :
https://t.co/KlVSTjKcp6
soon after it was launched.

Later, the AAP member alleged that the government took down his website, a claim that was later found to be false. It has now come to light that the users who trusted Abhijeet Dipke with their personal information have now been left vulnerable at the hands of potential cybercriminals.

On Wednesday (1st July), OSINT expert Nisarga took to X (formerly Twitter) to expose vulnerabilities on the website of the Cockroach Janta Party.

Earlier in its brief existence, the site was live and then responded with standard HTTP 403 errors from Hostinger’s active servers before the hold took effect.

In domain management terms, “clientHold” is a standard EPP (Extensible Provisioning Protocol) status code controlled exclusively by the registrar, not by governments or external authorities. According to ICANN documentation and registrar policies, this status instructs the registry not to publish the domain in the DNS, effectively taking it offline until the registrar resolves the underlying issue. Such instruction can be issued only by the owner of the website, not third parties, not even governments. Alternately, the domain provider or the host can take the website offline due to various reasons.

It is commonly applied for routine administrative reasons such as incomplete WHOIS contact verification, billing or payment problems, compliance violations, or at the request of the domain owner. The clientHold affects resolution globally at the registry level, not at any country level.

On the other hand, when a government orders blocking a website, it is done through ISPs (Internet Service Providers) in the country, and the block only takes place in that country. In India, such a block is typically enforced through the Department of Telecommunications via ISP-level DNS poisoning, IP blacklisting, or URL filtering. Such actions allow the domain to still resolve correctly on international resolvers outside the country. That is why websites blocked by the Indian govt can be accessed in India through VPN.

Moreover, when one visits a website blocked by the govt, the browser displays a message saying the same. But when one visits cockroachjantaparty’s website, the browser displays the code DNS_PROBE_FINISHED_NXDOMAIN. This means the browser can’t find the domain because it has been deactivated.

Moreover, no public government orders, court directives, or official statements have been issued regarding https://t.co/n5u5L8JbZ5, further undermining the censorship claim.

Therefore, the analysis of the website shows that either it has been taken by Dipte himself, or the domain provider/host took it down due to some compliance issues. There is no evidence that the site was taken down on Indian government’s order.

The meeting was also joined by Dr Parvinder Maini, Scientific Secretary.

Prof. Sood emphasised the importance of the LCA framework and the application developed under the project. He noted that these tools can provide Urban Local Bodies (ULB) with a science-backed basis for planning and support their transition towards smart, resilient and low-emission solid waste management systems across the country. Dr Maini highlighted the project’s alignment with the Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban and stressed the need for institutional mechanisms that can support the wider implementation of such solutions across the country.

Aligned with the vision of the Swachh Bharat Mission-Urban, Office of the PSA supported the project in 2024, which was jointly undertaken by @iiscbangalore, @iitmadras, and @IITBHU_Varanasi. The project consortium included key research of Life Cycle Assessment (LCA) modelling, greenhouse gas (GHG) accounting, and digital tool development. Along with them representatives from ULB based in Delhi and Bangalore also participated in the meeting. A demonstration video of the GHG calculator app showcased its key features and how it can help ULBs quantify emissions associated with different SWM technologies and operating scenarios.

A complete stranger slapped my teammate. I was next ! 

Today marks the day, almost a decade ago, when a group of 50 brokers attacked NoBroker. It was not the extent of the assault, but the surprise/shock of “Is it really happening?” What seemed like a local procession in front of our office-cum-residential house quickly revealed itself to be a group of people hell-bent on beating us and breaking computers/servers.

I ducked the next slap that was meant for me. When I tried to record it on my phone, it was quickly noticed by them. Our only saviour was the iron grill door through which we locked ourselves inside. Akhil and I had the look of “Ab kya karey?” on our faces. Next scene was us sitting in a police jeep going to the station, with brokers still continuing to create a ruckus at the office. We realised our complete lack of “connections,” with no IAS, IPS or politician on our speed-dial.

The day somehow ended, but the circumstances ensured that we had to vacate our office overnight and display “regret” messages on our website. Through the entire ordeal, somehow, it never crossed the minds of us three founders that NoBroker was at risk. Such is the power of optimism (or should I say misplaced innocence). Somehow, we struggled, the team grew stronger together, and we tried to survive one day at a time. 

Today, after Rs. 1,000 crore+ of yearly revenue and after serving 4 crore customers and saving thousands of crores in brokerage, we can afford to reminisce about it as an “incident” that happened. What did it teach us? Perseverance, optimism, the power of compounding and, above all, the power of “never giving up.”

text:
Two Thirds Still Back Fuel Demonstrators As Squeeze Tightens and Pump Prices Soar

This week on The Tonight Show, Shane Coleman noted that the April fuel protests nearly brought the country to a standstill and that two thirds of people now say “let’s do it again.” Michael Fitzmaurice TD added that two thirds of people are hurting. Those figures line up with what organisers already heard on the ground.
Public support was visible well beyond the polls. 

At the Tullamore Show in August, protest figures Christopher Duffy, James Geoghegan and John Dallon were repeatedly approached by attendees for photos and messages of thanks. Crowds told them the April action had given people hope. One woman said it was the first time in years she felt something might change. Relatively few people sought out the Taoiseach. When Duffy tried to put a calm question to Micheál Martin about fuel costs, gardaí and security surrounded him, grabbed his arm and briefly detained him. He was not arrested, but the message was clear: questions from people with concern were not welcome.

SnD Media’s news clips from Tullamore agri show garnered over 4.2 million views and more than 5,000 comments, most of them outraged and concerned at the growing frustration and the lack of engagement by publicly elected representatives. Those comments were noted and discussed by senior government TDs. Decisions followed to postpone reapplying the tax measures taken off after the pressure in April. We are now seeing a huge spike in these clips again.

The same pattern repeated this week at the National Ploughing Championships in Screggan. Farmers there spoke of overheads being wiped out by fuel and predicted more protests. A Roscommon farmer in his 60s tried to approach Martin to raise the issue. He was arrested under the Public Order Act shortly after midday on Tuesday, charged and released to appear in court later. Gardaí said no one was injured. Security around politicians was stepped up afterwards.

Pump prices are already matching or beating last April’s peaks. The average for diesel is around €2.05 a litre, with some stations hitting €2.14.9. SnD Media recorded a Certa pump outside Navan jumping from €1.96 to €2.08.9 overnight, a 12-cent rise. On the Navan Road leaving Dublin, two Circle K stations directly across from each other were 6 cent apart: €2.08 on one side and €2.14 on the other. Circle K in Cabra had diesel at €2.08.9; the same pump was €1.90 a week and a half ago, an 18-cent jump. 
On Tuesday a customer reported driving past a station in Bailieborough, Co Cavan, at €2.03; half an hour later it was €2.07. The same day Ardee was reported at €2.12

Rural businesses that cannot switch off their engines are still under pressure. Many agricultural contractors are already down thousands and simply cannot get paid, because the farmers do not have it. After a particularly dry summer, one of the hottest and driest on record, with grass growth collapsing and second and third cuts slashed, crop and fodder yields are down and cash has dried up on farms. 
Contractors who ran machines on credit through harvest are now carrying the debt. 

Haulage is in the same bind. Fuel already accounts for close to half of operating costs, and nearly half of licensed operators run just one truck. Tolls, insurance and port charges sit on top of diesel that many firms now call unviable. The government has already delayed tax increases once out of fear of a repeat. 

If the squeeze continues, the same networks that blocked the refinery and the motorways in April will be back on the roads. The reception at Tullamore and the arrest at the Ploughing show both the depth of public backing and how little official engagement there has been.
Nationwide demonstrations are not a distant risk. They are the likely next step.

text:
The Bombay High Court has strongly criticised the Maharashtra government's decision to impose a blanket alcohol ban in Pune district for 12 days during the Ganesh Chaturthi festival, questioning why the restriction was applied only in one district. A division bench of Chief Justice Mahesh Chandra Tripathi and Justice Advait Sethna said such orders could not assume that every person who drinks alcohol would create a law and order problem, and that action could instead be taken against anyone who actually causes trouble, regardless of whether they had consumed alcohol. The court was hearing petitions filed by associations representing hotel and wine shop owners, including the National Restaurant Association of India, challenging the Pune Collector's order that was scheduled to take effect from September 14. The bench asked the Collector's advocate to clarify whether the order would be withdrawn, warning that appropriate judicial action would follow if it wasn't. The judges also pointed out that keeping the entire district dry for so many days could lead to health issues for habitual drinkers, remarking in a lighter vein that hospitals could see a rush of patients if alcohol suddenly became unavailable. The matter is expected to be taken up again later in the day.

text:
They threw Black soldiers in prison for the dap, then turned around and begged them to teach it. Late in the Vietnam War, Black GIs were coming home inside their own minds, and they would not trust a white doctor to touch them. So the same military that banned the handshake brought in men fluent in it to dap with the wounded until they would accept help.

The thing they called a threat became the only bridge left to their own broken men, and that should sit with you for a long minute.

Two young men stand close in the heat, and for a moment their hands do something private. Fingers hook into fingers, knuckles meet knuckles, an open palm lands flat against a chest, and the whole exchange is over before a third man could follow it.

From any distance it looks like nothing at all. A greeting between friends, the kind of small motion you stop noticing by the second week in country.

But this was Vietnam, and these were Black soldiers, and what passed between their hands was not nothing. It was a promise, and on some bases it was treated as a crime.

The Black soldiers of that war had a name for themselves. They were the Bloods, and the dap was theirs.

The word is short and percussive, and it sounds a little like the thing it names. It could be plain, a bump and a clasp and done, or it could run long, dozens of moves strung in sequence, finished with a hand pressed over the other man's heart.

No two daps were exactly the same. The order of the moves shifted from one unit to the next, so that the way a man dapped could tell you who he had served beside.

That was the thing the men above them missed. The dap was never only hello.

It was a language, and it carried real weight. A run of movements could pass along what was waiting at the front, or what had gone wrong on the last patrol, moving hand to hand in plain sight where no officer could read a word of it.

Underneath all of it sat one sentence, repeated every time two of them met. I see you, I have you, we go home together or we do not go home.

That sentence existed because it had to. Black men were being funneled into the hardest corners of the war, and early on they were dying at rates well beyond their share of the men sent over.

And there were stories that moved quietly between them, of Black soldiers losing their lives not to the enemy but to white Americans in the same uniform. Whether every account held up or not, the fear behind them was real, and a man learned to count the people he could trust on the fingers of one hand.

So they made a pact. Not on paper, where it could be taken from them, but in their hands, where no one could.

There is a translation of the dap that survived into the museums, set down by the men themselves. The movements, they said, meant something close to this.

I am not above you. You are not above me, we stand side by side, we are together.

You will hear it said that the word stands for dignity and pride. The honest answer is plainer and a little lost to time, because no one is certain where the word truly came from, and that meaning may have been laid over it years later.

Some trace the snap and the clasp all the way back across the ocean to West Africa, to greetings that were old before any of these men were born. Whether the line runs that deep or not, what these soldiers built with it was new and entirely their own.

You do not need the dictionary to feel what it did. In a war that counted them as expendable, two Black men could reach out and hand each other their full human worth in under ten seconds.

To see the world that grew this thing, look at a place the soldiers called LBJ. The letters stood for Long Binh Jail, an Army stockade on the edge of Saigon, and the men inside lived under the bitter joke of a President's initials hanging over their cages.

It was built to hold four hundred. By August of 1968 it was packed with seven hundred and nineteen.

Black soldiers were about one in nine of the troops in Vietnam. Inside that jail, they were more than half of everyone there.

The worst cells were old steel shipping containers baking in the sun. A man could be locked inside one stripped to the skin, in heat well past a hundred degrees, a bare light left burning over him around the clock.

The summer of 1968 was already a wound that would not close. Word had reached the prison that Dr. King had been killed back home, and something in the men hardened that never fully softened again.

Into that place, the year before, had come an eighteen-year-old named Jimmie Childress. A judge had offered him a choice between prison and the Army, and he chose the Army, which is how a teenager ends up jumping out of airplanes with the 101st Airborne.

He fought, and then he stopped believing in the fight, and slipped away into a Saigon neighborhood where Black GIs gathered off duty. When they caught him and dropped him into LBJ, the thing that gnawed at him was not the cell itself.

It was the math of his own life. Long after, he still carried the question that would not leave him, why he should lay his body down for a country that would not let him sit at a lunch counter when he came home.

He was one man. The handshake belonged to thousands like him, and historians point to jails like this one, where the unfairness was stacked the highest, as one of the places the dap took its shape.

Here is where the story turns, and where it should make you stop scrolling.

That same year, the raised fist of Black Power had gone up on a podium at the Mexico City Olympics for the whole world to see. The military had already grown afraid of that fist, and had moved to ban its symbols wherever Black and white troops were packed in close.

Officers looked at the closed fist that ended the dap, and the long coded runs they could not crack, and they did not see men greeting each other. They decided they were watching the first moves of a Black uprising inside their own ranks.

So they banned a handshake. They wrote it up as a threat to good order and discipline.

And then they punished men for it. On bases from Vietnam to Germany to Hawaii, across the late sixties and into the seventies, Black soldiers were charged, court-martialed, jailed, and some were pushed out of the service with the kind of discharge that trails a man for the rest of his life.

Sit with the full shape of that. A young Black man could be handed a weapon, shipped to the other side of the planet, and ordered to die for the United States, and that same country would punish him for the way he said hello to the only people who had his back.

They did it anyway. Out in the open, daring the write-up, because every order against the dap only proved the one thing the dap was built to say.

The ban did not end it. It made it matter more.

And then comes the part almost no one was ever told, the part that turns the whole thing over in your hands.

Later in the war, the military that had been jailing men for the dap found that it suddenly needed it. There were Black soldiers coming apart from what they had carried, men who would not let a white doctor or nurse near them, because they no longer trusted anyone in that uniform to mean them any good.

So the Army went and found Black GIs who were fluent in the dap, and sat them down with these men, hand to hand, until enough trust was built for the wounded to accept treatment. The gesture they had branded a threat became the only bridge left to their own broken soldiers.

They could ban it. They could never replace it.

The dap should have died in a stockade outside Saigon. Instead it caught a flight home.

It came back in the hands of every man who made it out, and it spread the way only a true thing spreads. It traveled through blocks and barbershops and schoolyards and locker rooms, until a clasp of hands born as a survival code in a war zone became the ordinary, daily, almost unconscious way that Black America says I see you.

Now it lives everywhere. It is on the hardwood before tipoff, in the doorway when family arrives, between two strangers who catch something familiar in each other on a crowded street.

Decades later, a photographer named LaMont Hamilton went looking for what the record had let slip. He sat with old Black veterans and asked them to show him their daps, and he found the handshakes still changed from one former unit to the next, each one a small living museum of men who had been there.

And this is the last hard truth in it. The handshake conquered the world, and the men who built it mostly did not.

Their names were never written down. There is no wall anywhere carved with the list of who first hooked his fingers into another man's and decided that the gesture was a vow.

But the vow is still sitting in your hands. Every time you reach out and someone reaches back, knuckles to knuckles, you are finishing a sentence that frightened, furious, faithful young men began in a place that wanted them gone.

They were not allowed to keep their names. They kept their promise instead, and they handed it forward to you.

The next time someone daps you up, hold on a half second longer. Know exactly what it is you are holding.

I put a lot of effort into researching and sharing stories that matter.

Every coffee helps me keep creating

text:
The Supreme Court will not answer this fall how long the government may hold a lawful resident without a bond hearing.

The case was Genalo v. Black, and it asked whether the immigration statute's mandatory detention rule allowed a green card holder to be held for twenty-one months without a bond hearing.

The justices dismissed it as moot this month, after one man under the rule left the country and another received a pardon from New York's governor, which ended his deportability.

Believe it or not, it happened, because the question the Court was to settle was taken off the docket by a pardon and a departure rather than by a ruling.

It used to be called tyranny when power held a man beyond the reach of a judge.

The rule that earned the name was written down by a French judge who spent his life asking why some nations keep their laws while others lose them.

He held that a legislature which lets the executive imprison men who could answer for their conduct has ended liberty, and that an arrest may serve only to bring the man quickly to answer.

What matters is the hearing's speed, because a man brought before a judge in time is held by law, while one kept for twenty-one months without a hearing is held by discretion.

These men had been convicted of crimes, and the statute does command their detention, and yet a law enforced by keeping a man from ever asking a judge is not the rule of law.

A man held on the state's word alone is held by power and not by law, and the next case should get the answer this one missed.

"If the legislature leaves the executive power in possession of a right to imprison those subjects who can give security for their good behaviour, there is an end of liberty; unless they are taken up, in order to answer without delay to a capital crime, in which case they are really free, being subject only to the power of the law." — Montesquieu, The Spirit of the Laws, Book XI, ch. 6 (1748)

Date: 25th July 2026 

TO:

1. THAT recently, a digital broadcast / video recording was published and circulated on social media platform Instagram at (URL-https://t.co/23wqH3iWHY),featuring you, the unidentified Noticee (Jane Doe).

1.1 THAT in the aforementioned video broadcast, you have publicly uttered, performed, and disseminated statements/actions that are defamatory, inciting public mischief, & outraging public sentiments , hereby causing grave injury to public peace .

2. Your acts and public utterances attract strict criminal liability under BNS, 2023, specifically under:

   b) Section 353 (Public Mischief & Incitement to commit offenses against public tranquility);
   c) Section 356 (Defamation & Damage to Reputation);
   d) Section 299 / 196 (Outraging religious sentiments / Promoting enmity between classes, if applicable).

2.1 The electronic transmission and public hosting of the impugned content violates Rule 3(1)(b) of the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021, imposing a mandatory duty on platform intermediaries to disable access to objectionable digital material.

In light of the statutory breaches detailed above, you are hereby called upon to comply with the following requisites within SEVEN (7) DAYS from the date of this Notice:
A. CEASE AND DESIST- Immediately cease and desist from making, publishing, or propagating similar illegal, inflammatory, or defamatory statements/videos across any digital medium.

A copy of this Notice is retained in my office for future legal records and evidentiary reliance under Section 63 of the Bharatiya Sakshya Adhiniyam (BSA), 2023.

Shruti Dixit

Quackery-Unauthorized allopathic practice-Admission- Deposit of fine pending appeal-Competence to impose fine-. Drug-sale licence authorize only sale and distribution of drugs, not independent practice of medicine; recovery of used syringes/injections, coupled with the licence-holder's own admission of administering injections, established quackery. An unsubstantiated plea of coercion cannot rebut the presumption of regularity attaching to admissions recorded before a statutory body. The Hearing Committee, being the "Competent Authority" under the 2016 Regulations, is competent to impose fine under Section 28; voluntary deposit of fine without protest during pendency of appeal renders the appeal unmaintainable. Appellate judgment, having misread/overlooked these aspects, set aside; Hearing Committee's order restored

Timeline Of Rafale Mystery & A Saffron Chief Justice 

📍On 18 November 2016, the #Modi Govt told #Parliament that the cost of each #Rafale would be ₹670 crore.

📍On 31 December 2016, Dassault Aviation's annual report revealed that the actual price paid for each of the 36 aircraft was about ₹1,600 crore, more than twice what the #Modi Govt of India had said it was.

📍On 13 March 2017, Parrikar resigned as Defence Minister.

📍On 14 May 2017, Hollande's term as #French President ended.

📍On 13 March 2018, a PIL was filed in the #SupremeCourt which asked the #Modi Govt to disclose the transaction cost, and also asked why the Cabinet's approval was not sought as part of the Defence Procurement Procedure before signing the procurement deal with #France on 23 September 2016.

📍On 22 September 2018, Former French President Hollande was quoted in an interview as saying that it was the #Modi Govt that had insisted on Dassault partnering with #AnilAmbani for Rafale. 

📍The next day, 23 September, Hollande confirmed what he had said, and added that the name of #Reliance appeared as part of a 'new formula' by the #Modi Govt after it came to power.

📍On 10 October 2018, the #SupremeCourt asked the #Modi Govt to file in a 'sealed cover', details of the Rafale agreement.

⚠️ On 23 October 2018, at 2 a.m. in the morning, Modi divested #CBI chief Alok Verma of his powers, apparently after he showed interest in filing an FIR on the Rafale matter.

📍On 12 November 2018, the Union gave the pricing details in a 'Sealed Cover'.

📍On 14 December 2018, the #SupremeCourt dismissed all petitions asking the CBI to file an FIR in the deal. The bench, headed by CJI #RanjanGogoi.

📍On 2 January 2019, Jaswant Sinha, Arun Shourie and Prashant Bhushan moved court seeking a review of the 14 December judgement.

📍On 10 January 2019, the #SupremeCourt reinstated #CBI chief Alok Verma. 
⚠️ The next day, the #Modi Govt transferred him out of the #CBI and into the Fire Services.

📍On 14 November 2019, the #SupremeCourt dismissed the review pleas and said there was no need for an FIR.

💥 #RanjanGogoi retired three days later on 17 November, and was immediately appointed to the #rajyasabha. 

Thus Ended the Saga of the Rafale Deal.

text:
An extract from an article by Avay Shukla relevent to today's judgement on Swatantra  Bhardwaj bail-
'Jurisprudence in India today appears to be governed by four made-in-India/swadeshi doctrines which should be a blot on any justice system: fait accompli, sealed cover, ignore the science, and reward the criminal. Importantly, even constitutional challenges to the executive’s actions are kept on the backburner for so long (Article 370, CAA, SIR, Shiv Sena split) that by the time they are decided, it is impossible to turn back the clock and undo what the government of the day has already implemented on the ground.
The sealed cover has become the standard fallback option for denying full disclosure to civil society petitioners, or for not giving rebuttable reasons for a particular judgment (Rafale, Pegasus, Vantara, Hindenburg). Increasingly, this spectre of our swadeshi jurisprudence, like the executive, shows disdain and contempt for science, as in the case of stray dogs, Aravalli mountains, the Char Dham highway, and the Great Nicobar project. More trust is reposed on government-appointed committees and patently partisan ministries than on scientists, domain experts and specialised organisations working in the relevant field. Finally, this mutant form of justice also ensures that the criminal will be duly allowed to keep the proceeds of his crime (Ram Mandir theft, electoral bonds) even as his actions are declared irregular! A judicial paraprosdokian if ever there was one.'
Avay Shukla- Bumpy swadeshi model of justice.
The Tribune 19 July 2026

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

HOPE THAT HELPS

Comedian Kunal Kamra has filed a petition against the Centre's move to establish Fact-Check Units to identify and debunk 'fake and misleading' information about its functioning on social media platforms under the Press Information Bureau (PIB).

The online intermediaries would then have to take down such content if they wanted to retain their “safe harbour” (legal immunity against third-party content).

The Sacred and the Toxic: Constitutional Nihilism and the Death of the Yamuna

This video is ex facie documentary evidence of constitutional failure. The Yamuna, reduced to a toxic froth, stands as a mockery of Article 21. The Supreme Court in M.C. Mehta unequivocally held that the right to a clean environment is intrinsic to the right to life. Yet, for the women bathing in this poisonous lather, that fundamental right is a dead letter.

The legal record is damning. NGT penalties against the Delhi Jal Board and MCD are routinely stayed. The "Polluter Pays" principle remains a mere slogan. The Supreme Court’s suo motu cognizance of Yamuna pollution was abandoned, delegating the crisis to the NGT—a classic instance of judicial abdication. BOD levels at ITO bridge stand at 25 mg/l against a safe limit of 3 mg/l. This is not a natural calamity; it is a willful, man-made tragedy.

We are constrained to draw a stark parallel: the State’s investigative machinery awakens with alacrity when unaccounted cash is found in a minister's house. But when thousands of litres of industrial poison flow into the Yamuna daily, why is no one held accountable?

Articles 48A and 51A(g) impose a binding constitutional duty on the State and citizens to protect the environment. A duty without a sanction is a legal fiction.

We demand immediate contempt proceedings against the senior officials of the Delhi Jal Board and MCD for willful disobedience of NGT orders. We demand the strict, uncompromising enforcement of the "Polluter Pays" principle. The Constitution does not permit the State to drown its citizens in poison while hiding behind procedural delays.

The Yamuna is dying. The law must intervene, or it stands indicted alongside the State.

INDIA CRACKS DOWN ON AI & DEEP FAKE. BIG TECH PUT ON NOTCE

1. What has actually changed?

The Modi government amended the Information Technology (Intermediary Guidelines and Digital Media Ethics Code) Rules, 2021 on 10 February 2026 specifically to deal with synthetically generated information and deepfakes.
The framework covers deceptive AI-generated audio, visual and audio-visual material.
The idea is no longer simply: remove illegal content after somebody complains.

Platforms are now being pushed towards:
identification
labelling
metadata
verification
automated detection
rapid takedown
and greater accountability for allowing unlawful AI content to spread.

2. AI CONTENT HAS TO BE IDENTIFIABLE
This is probably the biggest structural change.
AI-generated/synthetically altered material covered by the rules has to be clearly identifiable as synthetic.
Platforms/services enabling generation or alteration of such content must ensure appropriate labels or traceable identifiers/metadata.
The objective is simple:
REAL CONTENT ≠ AI CONTENT
The viewer should not have to conduct a forensic investigation to figure out whether something was artificially generated.
Important nuance

Don't say “every piece of text written using AI anywhere on the internet must carry a label.”

MeitY's FAQ clarifies that the operative 2026 SGI definition primarily targets audio, visual and audio-visual information, not ordinary AI-generated written text.
A more accurate line for your video is:
“India has mandated identification and labelling requirements for covered AI-generated synthetic media, particularly deepfake audio, images and video.”

3. THE BIG NUMBER: 36 HOURS → 3 HOURS

Previously, once an intermediary received legally valid knowledge of unlawful material through the prescribed government/court process, the compliance window could be 36 hours.

That has now been cut to:

3 HOURS

That is a 91.7% reduction in response time.

So something capable of going viral nationally during an election, riot, communal incident, stock-market panic or national-security crisis can no longer theoretically remain online for a day and a half after a valid takedown direction.

The platform has only hours.

4. AND SOME COMPLAINT WINDOWS ARE EVEN SHORTER

The government says timelines for grievance redressal have also been compressed.

According to the PIB explanation:
certain complaints earlier subject to 72 hours can now require action within 36 hours

particularly sensitive categories that earlier had a 24-hour timeline can now require action within 2 hours

This specifically matters for areas such as:

impersonation

intimate imagery

nudity

deepfake abuse

other highly sensitive material.

5. BIG TECH CAN'T JUST WAIT FOR A COMPLAINT

This is another major change.

The government says intermediaries must deploy reasonable and appropriate technical measures, including automated tools or other mechanisms, against unlawful synthetically generated content.
That means platforms are increasingly being pushed from:
REACTIVE MODERATION
to
PROACTIVE DETECTION
For Significant Social Media Intermediaries, the framework explicitly envisages technical measures to identify prohibited content, including certain forms of:

rape-related material

child sexual abuse material

repeat prohibited content

unlawful synthetic content.

6. USERS MAY HAVE TO DECLARE AI CONTENT

The synthetic-media framework also places responsibility upstream.

Major platforms can be required to ask users uploading covered content whether it is synthetically generated and then use technical systems to check that declaration.

So theoretically:
User uploads video →
declares AI/not AI →
platform checks →
synthetic material gets labelled.

The earlier draft framework explicitly envisaged this declaration + technical-verification model.

7. WHY THE METADATA PART MATTERS

A visible watermark can be:

cropped,
blurred,
edited,
screen-recorded,

reposted.

Metadata/identifiers create another layer of traceability.

The government's objective is therefore not merely:

“PUT AI GENERATED IN THE CAPTION.”
It is building a system where synthetic content can carry technological indicators allowing platforms to recognise what it is.
That becomes especially useful once the same manipulated video is downloaded and re-uploaded across multiple platforms.
8. THE RULES TARGET DEEPFAKE IMPERSONATION DIRECTLY
Existing IT Rules already prohibit users from publishing material that:

impersonates another person

misleads users about the origin of a message

knowingly spreads patently false or misleading information

threatens public order

violates another applicable law.

AI does not create an exemption.

If AI is being used for impersonation, fraud, defamatory fabrication or other unlawful activity, existing criminal and cyber provisions can also apply.

9. BNS CAN ALSO COME INTO PLAY
The PIB release specifically points towards provisions of the Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita.
Depending upon what the deepfake is being used for, authorities could examine provisions relating to:
Section 319 — cheating by personation
Section 336 — forgery

Section 353 — false information/rumours capable of causing public mischief or fear

Section 111 — organised crime, where the factual circumstances justify it.

So there isn't necessarily a standalone offence called simply:

“making a deepfake.”

The legal consequence depends heavily upon what the deepfake does.

10. CHILD SEXUAL ABUSE DEEPFAKES GET SPECIAL ATTENTION
This is perhaps the least discussed but most important provision.
The amended framework explicitly covers harmful AI-generated material involving:
child sexual exploitation

non-consensual intimate imagery

impersonation

other prohibited synthetic material.

Platforms are expected to prevent such content and act rapidly when detected.

11. SOCIAL-MEDIA GIANTS HAVE EXTRA DUTIES

Platforms classified as Significant Social Media Intermediaries, broadly those crossing the prescribed Indian user threshold, face additional compliance obligations.

These include mechanisms involving:
automated detection
grievance officers
compliance officers

local points of contact

India-based compliance structures

periodic compliance reports

appeals processes

originator tracing in specified circumstances for messaging services.
So the rules are aimed not only at the person creating the deepfake.
They put a major compliance burden on the distribution network itself.
12. THE REAL STICK: SAFE HARBOUR
This is where it becomes serious for Meta, X, Google, Telegram and other intermediaries.
Section 79 of the IT Act provides intermediaries conditional protection from liability for third-party content.
But that protection depends upon complying with the law and prescribed due diligence.
The PIB release reiterates that failure to observe obligations under the IT Rules can result in the intermediary losing its Section 79 exemption, after which liability can arise under applicable law.

That makes the real equation:

Comply with due diligence → retain intermediary protection

Ignore statutory obligations → safe-harbour protection can be jeopardised

That is far more powerful than merely issuing a fine.

13. GOVERNMENT HAS BUILT A TAKEDOWN PIPELINE

There is now an increasingly integrated enforcement architecture:

Grievance Appellate Committees — GACs

Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre — I4C

SAHYOG Portal

National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal

police/cybercrime units

authorised State and Central Government agencies.

The SAHYOG system in particular enables centralised electronic communication of lawful content-removal notices to intermediaries.

14. INDIA IS ALSO BUILDING ITS OWN DEEPFAKE-DETECTION TECHNOLOGY

Under the IndiaAI Mission's Safe & Trusted AI pillar, government-backed work includes indigenous detection and governance technologies.
PIB identifies projects including:
Saakshya — multi-agent deepfake-detection framework developed by IIT Jodhpur and IIT Madras
AI Vishleshak — audio-visual forgery detection
IIT Kharagpur work on real-time voice deepfake detection.

So this is not purely a legal crackdown.

It is simultaneously a:

LEGAL + PLATFORM + TECHNOLOGICAL framework.

15. WHY THIS IS HAPPENING NOW

Generative AI has destroyed the old assumption that:
“Seeing is believing.”
Today one person can manufacture:

a politician announcing something he never said

a CEO apparently moving a stock

an Army officer issuing a fake warning

communal speeches

celebrity pornography

fake financial endorsements

fabricated battlefield footage

false evidence of violence
within minutes.
And the fake can reach millions before conventional fact-checking catches up.
Therefore the Indian approach is increasingly:
IDENTIFY → LABEL → DETECT → TRACE → REMOVE → PROSECUTE
rather than merely:
WAIT → RECEIVE COMPLAINT → INVESTIGATE.
THE BIG STORY FOR YOUR VIDEO

The headline isn't simply:

“Deepfakes must carry labels.”

The bigger story is that India is trying to change where responsibility lies.

Earlier, platforms could largely argue:

A user uploaded it; we are merely the intermediary.

The regulatory direction is increasingly:

If you operate the technology that generates, distributes or algorithmically amplifies synthetic content in India, you have duties to identify it, label it and respond rapidly when it becomes unlawful.

🚨 BIG: Government of India has unveiled one of the most comprehensive legal frameworks to combat AI-generated deepfakes, synthetic media, misinformation and unlawful online content.

The framework brings together the IT Act, 2000, Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita (BNS), 2023, IT Rules, 2021, the 2026 IT Rules amendments, and the IndiaAI Governance Guidelines to strengthen digital safety and platform accountability.

Key highlights:

🔹 Mandatory AI Labelling: Platforms must clearly label AI-generated or synthetic content with traceable metadata so users can identify manipulated content and prevent deception.

🔹 Fastest Takedown Timelines Yet: Removal of unlawful content after a valid government or court notice has been reduced from 36 hours to just 3 hours. Grievance redressal timelines have also been tightened—from 72 hours to 36 hours, and 24 hours to 2 hours for sensitive content such as nudity, impersonation and similar categories.

🔹 IT Act, 2000: Covers penalties for computer-related offences, identity theft (Sec. 66C), online impersonation (66D), privacy violations (66E), publishing obscene or sexually explicit content (Secs. 67 & 67A), empowers blocking of unlawful content under Sec. 69A, removal directions under Sec. 79, and enables police investigation under Secs. 78 & 80.

🔹 Bharatiya Nyaya Sanhita, 2023: Covers cheating by personation (Sec. 319), forgery through false electronic records (Sec. 336), spreading false reports or misinformation causing public mischief (Sec. 353), and organised cybercrime involving deepfake content (Sec. 111).

🔹 Strict Platform Obligations: Intermediaries must not host or share content that infringes rights, invades privacy, promotes hate or violence, harms children, violates intellectual property, misleads users about message origin, knowingly spreads false information, impersonates individuals (including using AI), threatens India's sovereignty, security or public order, or violates any applicable law.

🔹 Greater Accountability for Social Media Platforms: Significant Social Media Intermediaries (SSMIs) must assist law enforcement in tracing originators of serious content, deploy automated tools to detect unlawful content, publish compliance reports, appoint grievance and compliance officers, maintain India-based compliance infrastructure, and provide user verification, appeals and fair hearing mechanisms.

🔹 Zero Tolerance for Harmful AI: Platforms are now explicitly required to prevent AI-generated child sexual abuse material, non-consensual intimate imagery, deepfakes, AI impersonation, harmful synthetic media and other unlawful AI-generated content using reasonable technical measures and automated detection systems.

🔹 Legal Consequences: Failure to comply with the IT Rules can result in intermediaries losing their Section 79 safe-harbour protection, exposing them to prosecution and legal action under applicable laws.

🔹 Robust Enforcement Ecosystem: The framework will be enforced through Grievance Appellate Committees (GACs), the Indian Cyber Crime Coordination Centre (I4C), the SAHYOG Portal, the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, and law enforcement agencies. Citizens can report cybercrime and deepfakes through the National Cyber Crime Reporting Portal, with Helpline 1930 available for cyber fraud complaints.

🔹 Responsible AI Development: Under the IndiaAI Mission, the government is funding indigenous AI safety projects, including Saakshya (IIT Jodhpur & IIT Madras), AI Vishleshak, and IIT Kharagpur's Real-Time Voice Deepfake Detection System, alongside the India AI Governance Guidelines to promote safe, trusted and responsible AI deployment.

The message is clear: AI innovation is welcome, but deepfakes, impersonation, misinformation, child exploitation, and unlawful synthetic content will face significantly stricter regulation, faster takedowns, and stronger legal consequences than ever before.

People keep asking if President Trump can declare a national security emergency and cancel the midterms. Those are two different questions.

In August, Wayne Allyn Root suggested President Trump use an emergency declaration to push voter ID and proof of citizenship if the SAVE America Act doesn't pass. President Trump said “stranger things have happened.” He did not say he was canceling the midterms.

A national emergency is not a blank check. It only turns on powers Congress already wrote into law. There is no existing emergency power that lets a president cancel congressional elections. Congressional Election Day is set by federal law, and a president cannot unilaterally change it.

President Trump could declare an election-related emergency, and what it would actually do depends on which laws he cites. But no emergency declaration by itself gives a president the power to cancel the midterms. Anything beyond that is speculation, not fact.

A quick note for anyone pointing to Executive Order 13848. That is a national emergency President Trump declared in 2018 over foreign interference in U.S. elections, and he renewed it for another year on August 31. It authorizes sanctions against foreign actors involved in election interference. Renewing it does not add new powers, and it does not give a president the power to cancel, postpone, or take over an election.

# 🧾 Fact-Check System Prompt

**Version:** 0.5.0  
**Date:** 2026-09-11  
**Type:** System / context prompt  
**Created with:** Grok 4.6 (xAI)

---

## 📌 Usage (read this first)

Paste this entire document as the system / custom instructions.

Then send a separate user message that contains only the item to check. Do not put the target URL inside this prompt.

Accepted user-message formats:

1. URL only  
   https://t.co/23w27slz7i

2. Label + URL  
   Fact-check this:  
   https://t.co/23w27slz7i

3. Pasted post + optional URL  
   Caption: ...  
   URL: https://...

4. Screenshot / image of a post  
   Attach the image. Add the URL if you have it.

If the user message has a URL, open that URL first and fact-check that item.  
If both a URL and pasted text are present, the live URL is primary; pasted text is only a copy.  
If the user message has no URL, post text, or image, ask for one of those three. Do not invent a target.

If the user message is this document or a near-copy of it, reply only:  
`Target is the checker prompt itself. No check.`  
Do not fact-check this prompt.

---

You are a fact-checker. Check only what the author stated. Do not complete, defend, or rewrite the author’s argument.  
If a claim cannot be verified with available sources, say so. Do not guess.

## A. Quote first
Reproduce each claim in the author’s exact words.  
Separate: caption, image/overlay text, quoted third parties.  
Do not add motive or “what they must have meant.”

## B. Atomic claims
Split into the smallest testable units: actor, action, date, place, number, cause, comparison.  
A slogan is not a statistic. A target is not money spent.

## C. Allowed verdicts
Use only one per claim:
- True
- True but incomplete
- Aspiration presented as fact
- Unsupported
- False
- Rhetoric (not checkable)
- Unverifiable with available sources

Use **True but incomplete** only when the stated fact is correct *and* a material qualifier (scope, date, denominator, exception) is omitted that a reasonable reader would need.

If sources conflict, report the conflict. Do not pick a side to make the post coherent.

## D. Evidence rule
- True requires a primary source, official record, or named authority quoted contemporaneously, matching actor, number, date, and scope.
- The source must pre-date or independently document the event. A restatement issued after the post does not count.
- Goals, estimates, “eyes,” “will,” “set to,” and fundraising asks are not completed facts.
- Party, office, ideology, timing, or leadership is not proof that person ordered this action.
- Units, years, and geography must match.

## E. Attribution lock
“On X’s orders,” “because of X,” “X made this happen” is Unsupported unless a source shows X directed this action, figure, or document.  
Leadership status does not close that gap.  
Acceptable closer: a signed order, recorded instruction, or official document that names the actor and the specific action/figure.

## F. Novelty and contrast
“First,” “only,” “never before,” and “they do Y, we do Z” need comparative evidence. Otherwise: Unsupported or Rhetoric.

## G. Medium
Note satire, campaign handles, cropped screenshots, and edited graphics.  
If the only evidence is a cropped graphic or satire handle, default the claim to Unsupported or Rhetoric unless a primary source independently confirms it.  
Medium does not upgrade a weak claim to True.

## 📤 Output only
1. Item checked (URL or short description)
2. Quoted claims (caption vs image, listed separately)
3. One verdict + shortest evidence per claim, with source  
   Prefix each claim block with: `CLAIM n | VERDICT | SOURCE`
4. Conflicts or missing evidence, if any
5. The single source that would change an Unsupported causal claim to True

---

Parliament enacted the Promotion and Regulation of Online Gaming Act, 2025, prohibiting online money games. The 2026 Rules came into force from 1 May.

text:
Okay. Let me walk you through what happened.

On 31 August 2026, Malesela Teffo arrived at the Johannesburg High Court during Cat Matlala's attempted murder trial.

He was not on the case. He was not representing anyone. He walked in unannounced and asked to intervene — as a "friend of the court," or through his Pro Bono Foundation, claiming constitutional violations.

Judge Cassim Moosa told him to produce proof of readmission from the LPC or the High Court. Teffo could not.

The application was stood down.

Then the police arrived.

Here is what you need to understand before the headlines write themselves.

1. Teffo is not a lawyer anymore.

He was admitted as an advocate in 2009. But in September 2022, the Pretoria High Court struck him off the roll following an application by the Legal Practice Council.

The court cited serious professional misconduct: misappropriating client funds, taking briefs directly from clients without instructing attorneys, misleading courts, breaching court orders.

These were not allegations. These were findings of a court.

And in July 2026, he was acquitted of six criminal charges — assault, fraud-related matters, incidents from 2023. The LPC made clear: acquittal does not restore your right to practise. An acquittal says the state did not prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt. It does not erase a striking-off order.

He remains struck off. He is not entitled to appear in court or offer legal services.

2. The warrant was already in the system.

The LPC confirmed a warrant of arrest existed, stemming from a prior contempt finding. A 2023/2024 court order declared him in contempt of the original striking-off order, with a suspended 12-month imprisonment sentence if he complied.

Police had previously been unable to locate him.

Then he walked into a courtroom.

3. Now the context matters.

The trial he interrupted was Cat Matlala's — the same Vusimuzi "Cat" Matlala who won the R360 million SAPS medical tender that was later confirmed as irregular expenditure, with at least R50 million already paid before cancellation.

Matlala has been arrested on corruption and fraud charges. The charges against Police Commissioner Masemola linked to that tender were just dropped by the NPA.

Teffo is not a random bystander in this story.

He is a former defence counsel in the Senzo Meyiwa trial who gained prominence through that high-profile exposure. He positioned himself as a constitutional watchdog. And he showed up at the courtroom of a man whose tender was built on the same rot that the Madlanga Commission is currently mapping.

4. Here is the uncomfortable part.

A struck-off advocate appearing during a corruption trial does not raise the same question it would if the accused were a nobody.

When you remove yourself from the rolls of legal practitioners, when you are in contempt of the order that removed you, when a warrant is already circulating — and then you choose that moment to walk into that courtroom and ask to intervene...

The timing does not read like constitutional activism.

It reads like someone who knows which courtroom will get cameras.

5. That does not mean the constitutional questions he raised are wrong.

It does not mean the accused should not get a fair trial. It does not mean the state cannot abuse process.

But it does mean we should be clear about what this is.

It is not an advocate defending the rule of law.

It is a man who has been told by two separate courts that he cannot practise law, walking into a high-profile corruption trial and asking to be heard.

The judge did not hear him. The police did.

The uncomfortable truth:

The rule of law does not need protectors who are themselves subject to warrants.

A struck-off advocate appearing in court is not a constitutional crisis.

It is a man who forgot that the order striking him off was not a suggestion.

And the warrant that finally found him was not new.

It had been waiting.

#Teffo #CatMatlala #MadlangaCommission
